en: Thus have I heard: the Aggivacchagotta Sutta, the seventy-second discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, do you hold the view: ‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’?
“I do not hold such a view, Vaccha.”
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
“But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view: ‘The world is not eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’?”
“Vaccha, I do not hold the view:
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
“But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view: ‘The world is finite; this alone is true, all else is false’?”
“Does Master Gotama hold such a view?
“I do not hold such a view, Vaccha:
‘The world is finite; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
“But, Master Gotama, does Master Gotama hold the view: ‘The world is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false’?
“I do not hold such a view, Vaccha.”
“The world is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
“Master Gotama, do you hold such a view as this: ‘The soul and the body are one and the same; this alone is true, all else is false’?”
“Vaccha, I do not hold the view:
‘The soul is the same as the body; this alone is true, all else is false.
“But what then, Master Gotama, is it that ‘the soul is one thing and the body another; this alone is true, all else is false’?”
“Does Master Gotama hold such a view?
“I do not hold such a view, Vaccha:
‘The soul is one thing and the body another; this alone is true, anything else is false.’”
“Master Gotama, does Master Gotama hold the view: ‘A Tathāgata exists after death; this alone is true, anything else is false’?
“Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.”
‘The Tathāgata exists after death; this alone is true, all else is false.
‘But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view: “The Tathāgata does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false”?’
“Vaccha, I do not hold the view:
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.
“But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view: ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish’?”
“Does Master Gotama hold such a view?
“I do not hold such a view, Vaccha:
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; this alone is true, anything else is worthless.’”
“But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view: ‘A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish’?
“I do not hold such a view, Vaccha.”
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death;
this alone is the truth, all else is foolish’”—when asked, “Master Gotama, do you hold the view that ‘the world is eternal;
this alone is the truth, all else is foolish’? he replied, “Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.”
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false,” you say.
“But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view that ‘the world is not eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’?
Being thus asked, he replied: “No, Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.”
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false,’ you say.
When asked, ‘Master Gotama, do you hold the view that the world is finite; this alone is true, all else is false?’—being thus questioned, you replied: ‘No, Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.’”
"The world is finite; this alone is true, all else is false," you say.
"But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view: 'The world is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false'?
Being thus asked, he replied: "No, Vaccha, I do not hold such a view."
“The world is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
When asked, “Master Gotama, do you hold the view that ‘the soul and the body are one and the same; this alone is true, all else is false’?
being thus questioned, he replied: “No, Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.”
‘The soul is the same as the body; this alone is true, all else is vain,’ you say.
‘But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view that “the soul is one thing and the body another; this alone is true, all else is vain”?
Being thus asked, he replied: ‘No, Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.’
“The soul is one thing and the body another; this alone is true, all else is vain”—this is what you say.
“Master Gotama, when asked: ‘Does a Tathāgata exist after death? This alone is true, all else is vain’—does Master Gotama hold such a view?
Being thus questioned, he replied: “Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.”
‘The Tathāgata exists after death; this alone is true, all else is false,’ you say.
‘But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view that “the Tathāgata does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false”?
Being thus asked, he replied: ‘Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.’”
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is foolish,’ you say.
When asked, ‘Venerable Gotama, do you hold the view that “the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death;
this alone is true, all else is foolish”?’—being thus questioned, you replied, ‘Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.’”
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false’—do you say this?
‘But, Master Gotama, do you hold the view that “the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false”?
When asked thus, he said: ‘Vaccha, I do not hold such a view.’”
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish’—you say this.
But what fault, Master Gotama, do you see that you do not subscribe to any of these views at all?
“Vaccha, ‘the world is eternal’—this is a view, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a writhing of views.”
The proliferation of views and the fetter of views are accompanied by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever;
they do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
‘The world is eternal,’ Vaccha … ‘The world is finite,’ Vaccha … ‘The world is infinite,’ Vaccha … [and so on].”
‘The soul and the body are one,’ Vaccha...
‘The soul is one thing and the body another,’ Vaccha...
‘A Tathāgata exists after death,’ Vaccha... [and so on].
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ Vaccha—this is a speculative view, a thicket of views...
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ Vaccha—this is a speculative view, a thicket of views...
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ Vaccha—this is a speculative view, a thicket of views.
The wilderness of views, the thicket of views, the writhing of views, the fetter of views— accompanied by suffering, distress, despair, and fever—
is not conducive to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or nibbāna.
“Vaccha, it is precisely because I perceive this danger that I do not, in any way whatsoever, adhere to these various speculative views.
“But does Master Gotama hold any speculative view at all?
“‘Speculative view,’ Vaccha—this has been discarded by the Tathāgata.”
For this, Vaccha, has been seen by the Tathāgata:
"Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling, such its origin, such its passing away."
‘Such is perception, such is the arising of perception, such is the passing away of perception;
such are volitional formations, such is the arising of volitional formations, such is the passing away of volitional formations;
such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’”

“Therefore, Vaccha, I say that with the destruction, fading away, cessation, relinquishing, and giving up of all conceivings, all agitations, and all underlying tendencies to the conceits ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ the Tathāgata is liberated through non-clinging.
“But, Master Gotama, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, where is he reborn?
“‘He is reborn,’ Vaccha, does not apply.”
“In that case, Master Gotama, one is not reborn?
“‘One is not reborn,’ Vaccha, does not apply.
“In that case, Master Gotama, one both is reborn and is not reborn?”
“‘He both is reborn and is not reborn,’ Vaccha—this does not apply.
“In that case, Master Gotama, he neither is reborn nor is not reborn?
“‘He neither is reborn nor is not reborn,’ Vaccha—this also does not apply.”
“But, Master Gotama, when asked: ‘Does a bhikkhu whose mind is thus liberated reappear anywhere? you replied: ‘Vaccha, it does not fit to say that he reappears.
When asked: ‘Then, Master Gotama, does he not reappear? you replied: ‘Vaccha, it does not fit to say that he does not reappear. When asked:
‘Then, Master Gotama, does he both reappear and not reappear? you replied: ‘Vaccha, it does not fit to say that he both reappears and does not reappear.’”
“In that case, Master Gotama, when asked, ‘Does one neither reappear nor not reappear? you replied, ‘Vaccha, “one neither reappears nor does not reappear” is not applicable.
Here, Master Gotama, I have fallen into ignorance; here I have fallen into confusion.
Even that slight degree of confidence I had in Master Gotama’s previous conversation has now vanished.”
“Enough, Vaccha, of this ignorance; enough of this delusion.
For this Dhamma, Vaccha, is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.
It is difficult for you to realize it, being as you are of a different view, a different inclination, a different persuasion, following a different discipline, and having a different teacher.”
"In that case, Vaccha, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.
What do you think, Vaccha:
if a fire were burning in front of you, would you know: 'This fire is burning in front of me'?"
“‘This fire is burning in front of me,’ would you say?
“If, Master Gotama, a fire were burning in front of me, I would know:
‘This fire is burning in front of me.’”
“But if, Vaccha, someone were to ask you this:
‘This fire burning before you—what does it depend upon for its burning?’—being asked thus, Vaccha, how would you answer?
“If, Master Gotama, someone were to ask me this:”
“If you were asked, ‘This fire burning before you—what does this fire depend upon for its burning?’, being thus questioned, Master Gotama, I would answer:
‘This fire burning before me depends upon fuel consisting of grass and wood for its burning.
“Vaccha, if that fire before you were to go out, would you know: ‘This fire has gone out’?”
“‘This fire in front of me has gone out,’ would you say?
“If that fire in front of me, Master Gotama, were to go out, I would know:
‘This fire in front of me has gone out.’”
“But if, Vaccha, someone were to ask you this:
‘This fire that was burning in front of you has gone out;
in which direction did that fire go—from the east, or the south, or the west, or the north?’—being asked thus, Vaccha, how would you answer?”

“It does not apply, Master Gotama. For that fire, Master Gotama, which blazed up dependent on a supply of grass and wood, with the exhaustion of that fuel and the non-introduction of any other, is reckoned simply as ‘extinguished’ because it lacks nutriment.

“In the same way, Vaccha, whatever form by which one might designate a Tathāgata—that form has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising.
"Vaccha, the Tathāgata is liberated from the reckoning of form; he is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, just like the great ocean.
'He is reborn' does not apply; 'he is not reborn' does not apply; 'he is both reborn and not reborn' does not apply; 'he is neither reborn nor not reborn' does not apply."

Whatever feeling by which one might designate a Tathāgata— that feeling has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
Released through the destruction of feelings, Vaccha, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, just like the great ocean.
"It is reborn" does not apply; "it is not reborn" does not apply; "it is both reborn and not reborn" does not apply; "it is neither reborn nor not reborn" does not apply.

Whatever perception one might use to designate the Tathāgata, that perception has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
Released through the destruction of perception, Vaccha, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable.
It is just like the great ocean.
"He is reborn" does not apply; "he is not reborn" does not apply; "he is both reborn and not reborn" does not apply; "he is neither reborn nor not reborn" does not apply.

Those mental formations by which one might designate a Tathāgata have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.
"Vaccha, the Tathāgata, liberated through the destruction of the formations, is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable—just like the great ocean.
'He is reborn' does not apply; 'he is not reborn' does not apply; 'he is both reborn and not reborn' does not apply; 'he is neither reborn nor not reborn' does not apply."

That consciousness by which one might designate a Tathāgata has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future. Released from the exhaustion of consciousness,
Vaccha, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, just like the great ocean.

"It does not apply that 'he is reborn'; it does not apply that 'he is not reborn'; it does not apply that 'he both is reborn and is not reborn'; it does not apply that 'he neither is reborn nor is not reborn.
When this was said, the wanderer Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One:
"Just as, Master Gotama, there might be a great sāla tree not far from a village or a town..."
Just as the branches and foliage of that tree might decay, its bark and inner bark might decay, and its softwood might decay;
and at a later time, it would become pure, established in its core, with its branches and foliage gone, its bark and inner bark gone, and its softwood gone— just so,
the teaching of Master Gotama is pure, established in its core, with its branches and foliage gone, its bark and inner bark gone, and its softwood gone.
“Excellent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
The *Aggivacchasutta*, the second, is finished.
